terms.gloss: storey, floor of a building; also boarded flooring
terms.comment: The authors count storeys with ordinals (Livy’s tertia contignātiō, Juvenal’s tabulāta tertia), and do not say whether the ground floor counts. The reference works disagree: Traupman, counting the American way, has the ground floor (pedeplāna) and then the tabulātum secundum, the first floor up; Levi–Bini, counting the Italian way, call the ground floor tabulātum īnfimum, so their tabulātum secundum is two flights up. Martial’s way avoids the question: scālīs habitō tribus, I live up three flights.

terms.gloss: a floor, a storey (properly the joists and boards)

phrases.latin: et scālīs habitō tribus, sed altīs
phrases.english: and I live up three flights of stairs, and tall ones

phrases.latin: bovem in tertiam contignātiōnem suā sponte ēscendisse
phrases.english: that an ox had climbed of its own accord to the third storey

phrases.latin: Ūcalegōn, tabulāta tibi jam tertia fūmant: tū nescīs
phrases.english: Ucalegon is already smoking on the third floor below you, and you don’t know it

phrases.latin: Quattuor cubicula in pedeplānīs sunt; cētera in tabulātō secundō sunt.
phrases.english: There are four bedrooms on the ground floor; the rest are on the floor above.

phrases.latin: Avia ūnīs scālīs habitat, nōs tribus.
phrases.english: Grandma lives one floor up, and we live three.

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 121, 123, 125, 316, 386, 401.
Enrico Levi and Arturo Bini, Il latino come lingua viva (1937), p. 267.
